title: A shared services approach to administrative and back-office functions.
summary: Back-office support is treated as overhead, but it doesn’t have to be. Learn why outsourced shared services through a BPO partner makes it an advantage.
body_markdown:
### Key takeaways:


Drawn from Kelly Professional & Industrial™ experience managing shared services programs for global pharmaceutical companies:


- Back-office support, such as executive administrative support, purchase order (PO) processing, and contract administration, loses value when it depends on individuals and departmental silos.
- Outsourced shared services moves ownership of that work to a dedicated team managed by a partner, so managers receive support as a service instead of supervising it.
- Outsourced shared services makes a difference in five areas: strategy, consistent process, flexible capacity, measurable performance, and the experience of your people.
- The results are measurable. One global pharmaceutical program delivered more than $1 million in first-year savings, annual turnover under 10%, and open roles refilled in about 30 days.


**Less management, more performance: a shared services approach to administrative and back-office functions.**


I regularly connect with business leaders to discuss administrative and back-office support, and the pattern is remarkably consistent. Executive administrative support, purchase order (PO) processing, and contract administration rarely make the strategy agenda. They get treated as costs to manage, not levers to pull, and they get attention only when something breaks.


Nearly[40% of a manager’s day](https://fortune.com/2025/03/31/overwhelmed-managers-putting-out-fires-daily-tasks-admin-work-instead-planning-future/) goes to last-minute problems or administrative tasks, according to a global Deloitte survey of nearly 10,000 business and HR leaders.


When back-office support breaks, the cause is usually less about the people than about how the work is set up. Support that runs through departmental silos and individual contributors starts strong, but it has no cushion when conditions change. Any of these can break it:


- A spike in workload
- A shift in required skills
- A resignation
- A reorganization


Each one pulls managers away from the business or forces them to find budget for temporary help nobody planned for. Today, the variables are multiplying, making it even more difficult to adapt. AI, shifting business needs, workforce demographics, volatile markets, remote work, and global operations have all sped up the pace of change.


Organizations today are finding that they can get ahead of constant volatility when they stop patching individual roles. They outsource the actual business processes to a business process outsourcing (BPO) partner. That partner runs traditional administrative support, as well as purchase order (PO) administration, helping teams manage operational processes, documentation, approvals, tracking, and overall administrative coordination.


These capabilities are leveraged as needed, depending on the structure and needs of the business, leadership team, and project environment. Depending on those needs, the managed supporting team may include administrative assistants, executive administrative assistants, senior executive administrative assistants, project coordinators, and hybrid administrative/project coordinators.


The overall impact is a significant improvement in how support works across the business. Multiple distributed processes become a managed function with a dedicated team behind it. That's the outsourced shared services approach, and the following questions reveal how it makes a real difference.


### 1. Why aren't temporary staffing, virtual assistants, and extra coverage enough for back-office support?


Temporary staffing, virtual assistants, and extra coverage aren't enough because each one still depends on a single individual, so support loses value the moment the first variable hits. Without a way to stabilize it, leaders see back-office support as overhead and a standing risk. Managers end up running it: hiring, covering absences, checking work, and chasing follow-ups instead of leading the business.


It looks like a hiring problem, so people try to solve it with hiring. Repeatedly hiring workers one at a time to fill gaps in an undermanaged function treats a symptom. But it does not treat the cause, which is why the problem becomes overwhelming and costly.


When[ownership of back-office support moves to a partner](https://www.kellyservices.com/divisions/professional-industrial/expertise/bpo/) , people, development, resourcing, and process performance sit with a dedicated team. Your internal managers stop supervising the work and start receiving it as a service.


**When is a shared services model a good fit?**
A shared services model isn't right for every need, and sometimes a new hire or a contingent worker is the better call, particularly when filling an occasional need. The model delivers significantly more value when an organization has:


- **Persistent support challenges:** A cycle of repeated support disruption
- **A lack of reliable cost and performance data:** Disconnected **** internal functions hiding cost and performance gains
- **Leadership buy-in to a new solution:** Executives open to transferring ownership of their support functions to a shared services provider


### 2. How does shared services standardize back-office processes?


Shared services replaces the different ways each division, leader, and individual does the work with one standardized process, built through a phased transition. Without that dedicated management, quality and turnaround depend on who happens to be doing the work.


Contract and PO requests are the classic case: Intake differs by team, information gets requested twice, and follow-ups multiply. The documentation, approvals, tracking, and administrative coordination of those requests often suffer from inconsistency or are overlooked. A shared services team is built to provide that consistency for addressing every need, every time.


**What shared services puts in place.**


The transition runs in three steps:


1. Migrate the work to the managed team.
2. Remove redundancy.
3. Deliver through cross-trained specialists.


This phased approach can protect institutional knowledge while roles are restructured around the company's own systems and compliance requirements. As an example, consider standardizing contract and PO support — an unglamorous, but effective, tactic. For one pharmaceutical R&D group, our contracting team:


- Centralized intake
- Standardized project naming
- Kept a shared tracker
- Built a training deck


Our data showed each contract averaged almost 11 touchpoints from request to completion. You can only see, and improve, those steps once someone owns the process end to end.


Executive assistants at one life sciences company applied the same standardization across divisions: uniform contract-request intake, shared templates, advance review of calendars and deadlines, and regular status updates. The result was a reduction in delays, increased executive confidence, and improvement in team engagement and motivation.


### 3. How can back-office support flex with demand?


A shared services model lets back-office support scale up and down as demand shifts, with cross-training and coverage built in so absences don't create gaps. A fixed support ratio can leave an organization over- or under-resourced when demand changes. Shared configurations, such as 4:1 or 5:1, can and should be treated as options — not one-size-fits-all rules. Support can also be dedicated 1:1 or tailored to project and coordination needs.


**How the shared services model keeps support matched to the need:**


- Higher standards: Outcomes can be benchmarked against performance in comparable organizations. In a particular pharmaceutical example, that expectation has risen to $1 million in first-year savings, 90% retention, and a 30-day average to fill vacancies.
- Real-time visibility: Growth and reduction are tracked as they happen.
- Redeployment: When one company reduced headcount, experienced administrators were redeployed instead of lost. Of five administrators whose assignments ended over three years, three moved to other managed teams, and two were rehired into other programs.
- Coverage: Built-in continuity and backup support can make the difference in an effective shared services model. Cross-trained team members, peer-to-peer support, and a trainer/floater role help cover vacations, unplanned absences, backfill periods, and peak cycles. Delegate access and established processes enable trained shared resources to step in quickly, minimize disruption, and maintain continuous support.


### **4. How do you measure the cost and performance of back-office support?**


When managed internally through separate departments or locations, support services are rarely measured. That means no one can say whether those services are improving or what they really cost.


In a shared services model, cost and performance are measured through contractually tracked metrics and service levels, which turn support into a function that reports on itself and keeps improving.


**What shared services makes measurable.**


Typical measures include:


- Timeliness of response
- Quality
- Capacity
- Replacement time after turnover
- Turnover, tracked with cause
- Off-hours coverage
- Other metrics that align to the particular business


Outsourcing shared services also changes the financial picture of support work. Fixed costs like fringe and workers' compensation become variable. In one global pharmaceutical program, the model delivered more than $1 million in first-year savings and an annual turnover of less than 10%.


### 5. What happens to administrators and managers under shared services?


The worry I hear most is that outsourcing means pushing out good people, and strong administrators often have nowhere to grow in the first place. Done well, the impact of shared services is the opposite. Current administrators can transition into the managed team rather than being replaced.


**What outsourcing shared services means for people.**


Four advantages stand out:


- **Transition, not replacement:** In one conversion of 44 administrators, 19 joined us, and the remaining roles were filled within 30 days.
- **Real employment:** Administrators become full-time employees with benefits and paid time off.
- **Room to grow:** Administrators get development plans, ongoing professional development and skills enhancement, and structured onboarding and cross-training with peers. The model also includes an administrative certification program to strengthen executive support, organizational effectiveness, communication, project coordination, and business partnership capabilities.
- **Retention:** Contractors nearing a two-year tenure cap have joined the model, and some administrators have been in their roles for six to eight years.


Managers and leaders benefit, too. Peer mentoring shortened one team's onboarding to five to six weeks (down from eight to 10 weeks). Managers get reliable support, as well as time back from the lengthy onboarding processes, and leadership sees the effect on the bottom line.


**Turn back-office support from overhead into an advantage.**


Support functions look like overhead, because they're usually run like overhead: person by person, department by department, with managers as the shock absorber. Run as a managed service, they become a source of resilience, measurable performance, and cost advantage.


The question isn't whether to replace your administrative professionals. It's whether to keep asking them, and your managers, to absorb every variable alone. If any of these situations sound familiar,let’s talk . We’ll assess where your back-office support breaks down and show you what a managed shared services model could look like for your organization.
